claims.text: Machine learning–optimized dealloying can produce noble metal–based HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Machine learning–optimized dealloying provides controlled atomic distributions in NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
Machine learning–optimized dealloying enhances catalytic performance relative to conventionally processed NM-HEAs.
The proposed precursor is a homogeneous multi-element NM-HEA containing both noble and less noble metals.
In-situ alloying can be used to prepare the proposed NM-HEA precursor.
A machine learning model can guide selective leaching and optimize dealloying composition and process parameters.
The dealloying can be performed at ambient or mildly elevated temperature in an acidic or alkaline solution.
Solution concentration, temperature, and time can be tuned through data-driven predictions.
The process forms a porous, interconnected three-dimensional nanoframework with high surface area.
The resulting nanoframework has precise atomic-level arrangements.
Selective removal of less noble elements induces self-organized nanoporosity in the remaining noble-metal network.
Refined atomic structure creates or enhances catalytic active sites.
The optimized process yields uniform elemental distribution and tailored pore structure.
The resulting structures have measurably improved catalytic activity and stability compared with conventionally fabricated NM-HEAs.
Traditional synthesis methods such as melting or additive manufacturing often produce non-uniform atomic distributions.
Traditional synthesis methods provide less controlled nanoporosity than the proposed process.
The dealloying approach is limited to compositions with sufficiently different corrosion rates to permit selective leaching.
Element segregation can preclude uniform nanopore formation.
The magnitude and cross-system generality of the predicted catalytic improvement remain experimentally undetermined.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mediator state that dealloying itself produces the 3D nanoframework, whereas the falsification design says both samples are post-processed after dealloying to fabricate the nanoframeworks, making the framework-forming step ambiguous.
The stated baseline is NM-HEAs made by melting or additive manufacturing, but the experimental control is a conventionally optimized dealloying process; these are materially different comparators.
